ForceAssignExperiment.blurb: Forces AnkiLab (A/B testing) to treat this robot as belonging to a specific experiment variation. Takes two string arguments: experimentKey and variationKey (names from the lab definition, not free-form labels). Used by QA/dev to put a unit into a known treatment/control bucket without waiting for random assignment.
ForceAssignExperiment.detail: Registered under category “A/B Testing” in lib/util (shared by engine and anim). Handler reads experimentKey and variationKey, calls AddABTestingForcedAssignment, and echoes the pair to the console channel. That path enables A/B testing if it was force-disabled, then either (1) stores the pair in a static map if the AnkiLab op-runner is not wired yet, or (2) runs lab->ForceActivateExperiment(experimentKey, userId, variationKey) when the runner is live. ForceActivateExperiment validates keys against the loaded AnkiLabDef, refuses invalid experiment/variation names, and records a force assignment so IsActiveExperiment is true and later ActivateExperiment returns that variation. Engine wires the interface in CozmoExperiments::InitExperiments (user id = head serial when a robot exists, else device id). Experiments are loaded from config/experiments.json via RobotDataLoader. Anim process also registers the console function (same lib) but never calls InitializeABInterface, so pressing it on :8889 only fills a map nothing reads — use engine :8888 for real effect. Does not by itself rewrite product features unless code elsewhere consults that experiment.
ForceAssignExperiment.howTo: 1) Prefer engine console (:8888). 2) Look up valid keys/variations in resources/config/experiments.json (or whatever the robot loaded). 3) Call ForceAssignExperiment with experimentKey and variationKey. 4) Confirm log line “ForceAssignExperiment X => Y” and AnkiLab.ForceActivate if successful. Wrong names yield ExperimentNotFound / VariantNotFound (no force).

paths.notes: Robot loads experiments from the installed resources path (engine RobotDataLoader pathToResource …/config/experiments.json).

ForceAssignExperiment.statusNote: Live on engine after CozmoExperiments::InitExperiments (sOpRunner set). On anim, or before AB interface init, only a static map is written and GetABTestingForcedAssignments has no production readers — effectively a no-op. Invalid experiment/variation keys do nothing useful.

IntentionalAbort.blurb: Immediately aborts the process you call it on (engine on :8888 or anim on :8889). Logs IntentionalAbort then calls C abort(), which raises SIGABRT and usually produces a crash dump / Breakpad minidump. The robot will lose that process until systemd/watchdog restarts it.
IntentionalAbort.detail: Dev/QA fault-injection helper in lib/util ConsoleSystem (category “Debug”), compiled when REMOTE_CONSOLE_ENABLED (on for this rebuild’s dumps on both ports). Same binary path in engine and anim — press on the port of the process you intend to kill. No arguments. After abort the console session dies with the process; expect face freeze / motion stop if you kill eng or anim, and a restart cycle.
IntentionalAbort.howTo: Only on a robot you are willing to crash. Pick the correct process tab/port, call IntentionalAbort once, wait for restart. Do not use on a production unit in the field.
IntentionalAbort.statusNote: Hard-kills vic-engine or vic-anim via abort()/SIGABRT. Intentional fault injection only.

IntentionalAssert.blurb: Attempts to fire a failed C assert (assert(false)) in the process you call it on, after logging IntentionalAssert. On debug builds without NDEBUG this typically aborts like a failed assert. On VICOS Release toolchains that define NDEBUG, assert is compiled out so you may only see the log line and no crash.
IntentionalAssert.detail: Same shared Debug CONSOLE_FUNC family as IntentionalCrash. Use when testing assert-path crash reporting vs null-deref or signals. Because product Release flags include -DNDEBUG (vicos/android release toolchains), treat a “no crash” result as expected for assert, not as proof the button is broken — try IntentionalAbort or IntentionalCrash to force a real fault.
IntentionalAssert.howTo: Call on the target process. If the process stays up, check whether this firmware was built with NDEBUG and use IntentionalAbort/IntentionalCrash instead for guaranteed termination.
IntentionalAssert.statusNote: Danger when assert is live (debug). On NDEBUG/Release builds the assert body is stripped — logs then returns (partial effectiveness). Still never press casually.

IntentionalCrash.blurb: Deliberately crashes the process by writing to a null pointer (*(int*)0 = 42) after an IntentionalCrash log line. Used to test crash reporting, Breakpad, and process restart. Kills only the process behind the console port you hit (engine or anim).
IntentionalCrash.detail: Classic fault-injection entry in ConsoleSystem under “Debug”. volatile int* at address 0 guarantees a SIGSEGV-style fault independent of assert/NDEBUG. Immediate process death; no recovery until the service restarts. Anim crash freezes face/audio path; engine crash stops behaviors/actions until vic-engine is back.
IntentionalCrash.howTo: Select engine or anim console → IntentionalCrash. Expect process death and (if configured) a crash report. Prefer this over IntentionalAssert when you need a reliable crash on Release builds.
IntentionalCrash.statusNote: Null-pointer write; guaranteed process crash for fault-injection testing.

IntentionalExit.blurb: Calls exit(-1) on the process after logging IntentionalExit. Cleaner process termination than a segfault (runs atexit handlers / flushes in a normal exit path) but still ends vic-engine or vic-anim immediately with a failing status.
IntentionalExit.detail: Debug CONSOLE_FUNC with no args. Unlike IntentionalCrash/Abort this is a voluntary process exit rather than a signal fault — useful to compare “orderly” exit restart vs crash dump paths. Still takes down all robot functionality owned by that process until restart.
IntentionalExit.howTo: Call on the process you want stopped. Wait for systemd/service manager to bring it back. Do not use unless you intend to stop that process.
IntentionalExit.statusNote: Process exit(-1); stops engine or anim by design.

IntentionalMallocBigNum.blurb: Stresses the process heap by repeatedly malloc’ing large blocks (starts at 128 MB, halves on failure, down to 4 bytes), chaining successful blocks together and never freeing them. Goal is to exhaust memory or provoke OOM killer / allocation failures for stress testing.
IntentionalMallocBigNum.detail: Debug helper — does not free the chain. Can hang the console call for a long time while allocating, thrash the robot into swap/OOM, or leave the process critically low on memory even if it survives. Worse than a clean crash button because partial success can leave eng/anim unstable without an immediate restart. Prefer intentional crash/abort helpers if you only need a dump.
IntentionalMallocBigNum.howTo: Only on a disposable/dev robot with monitoring. Call once; watch free memory and logs for IntentionalMallocBigNum size lines. Expect possible OOM kill or need to restart the process afterward. Avoid on a unit you care about mid-session.
IntentionalMallocBigNum.statusNote: Unbounded allocate-and-leak loop; can OOM-kill or permanently bloat the process heap until restart.

IntentionalPthreadExit.blurb: Calls pthread_exit(NULL) on the thread that is handling the console function (after logging IntentionalPthreadExit). Ends that thread only — not necessarily the whole process — which can leave engine or anim half-dead (console dead, main loop stuck, or process aborted when the last thread exits).
IntentionalPthreadExit.detail: Unlike IntentionalExit/Crash, this is thread-scoped. Depending on which thread services remote console commands, you may hang the console channel, corrupt state, or still take the process down. Intended to exercise thread-exit / pthread cleanup paths, not as a clean stop. Prefer IntentionalExit or IntentionalSIGTERM for a full process stop.
IntentionalPthreadExit.howTo: Dev-only. Call once and observe whether the process dies, the console stops responding, or the robot becomes unresponsive. Plan to restart the process either way.
IntentionalPthreadExit.statusNote: pthread_exit on the console handler thread; can strand or kill the process unpredictably.

IntentionalSIGINT.blurb: raise(SIGINT) in the target process after logging IntentionalSIGINT. Same signal as Ctrl-C — typically terminates unless the process installs a SIGINT handler that ignores it.
IntentionalSIGINT.detail: Part of the Debug intentional-signal suite (SIGTERM/INT/QUIT/KILL). Useful to verify signal handling and service restart for interactive-interrupt style stops. Hits only the process bound to that console port.
IntentionalSIGINT.howTo: Call on engine or anim. Expect process stop and restart. Compare with SIGTERM/SIGKILL if handlers differ.
IntentionalSIGINT.statusNote: Sends SIGINT to the process; stops eng/anim for fault/restart testing.

IntentionalSIGKILL.blurb: raise(SIGKILL) on the target process after logging IntentionalSIGKILL. SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored — the kernel tears the process down immediately with no cleanup handlers.
IntentionalSIGKILL.detail: Harshest intentional signal helper. No atexit, no destructor-friendly shutdown: open files, IPC sockets, and locks vanish with the process. Use when testing “hard kill” recovery (systemd restart, anim/engine reconnect). Prefer SIGTERM first if you want a catchable stop.
IntentionalSIGKILL.howTo: Call once on the intended process port. Process is gone immediately; wait for service restart.
IntentionalSIGKILL.statusNote: Uncatchable SIGKILL; hard-kills the process with no cleanup.

IntentionalSIGQUIT.blurb: raise(SIGQUIT) after logging IntentionalSIGQUIT. Often used to quit with a core dump (like Ctrl-\). Terminates the process unless a custom handler intervenes.
IntentionalSIGQUIT.detail: Debug signal suite member. Behavior depends on process signal disposition and core-dump ulimits on the robot image. Useful alongside IntentionalCrash when comparing dump-producing paths.
IntentionalSIGQUIT.howTo: Call on engine or anim; expect quit (+ possible core). Restart the process after.
IntentionalSIGQUIT.statusNote: Sends SIGQUIT; can terminate with core dump depending on OS settings.

IntentionalSIGTERM.blurb: raise(SIGTERM) after logging IntentionalSIGTERM. Standard “please terminate” signal — catchable; default action is process termination. Mimics a polite service stop.
IntentionalSIGTERM.detail: Softest of the intentional kill signals (vs SIGKILL). Good for testing graceful-shutdown handlers if the process installs any; otherwise still exits. Only affects the process for the console port used.
IntentionalSIGTERM.howTo: Call on :8888 (engine) or :8889 (anim). Watch for clean exit vs hung shutdown, then restart if needed.
IntentionalSIGTERM.statusNote: Sends SIGTERM; stops the process unless a handler blocks it.

IntentionalThrow.blurb: Throws a C++ exception (throw "error") after logging IntentionalThrow. If nothing catches it on the console call stack, std::terminate runs and the process aborts — another crash-injection path distinct from signals and null deref.
IntentionalThrow.detail: Debug CONSOLE_FUNC. Exercises exception / terminate paths and any surrounding try/catch on the console dispatcher (if present). Uncaught exception → process death similar to abort. Prefer IntentionalCrash when you need a simple, predictable fault on Release builds.
IntentionalThrow.howTo: Call once on the target process. Expect terminate/abort if uncaught. Restart process after.
IntentionalThrow.statusNote: Uncaught C++ throw typically calls std::terminate and kills the process.
